outcome_analysis.explanation: The current completed official evaluations are not discordant: both parallel and serial failed with the same 31/70 result. Parallel's distinctive behavior was to delegate CLI and runtime discovery, consume both child reports, and then implement and repair the output tree in the parent. Serial did the work in one thread and included a non-ASCII probe and ASCII JSON serializer. The mounted evidence does not show a parallel coordination episode that explains a different official outcome; the remaining failures are shared or ordinary implementation/acceptance gaps whose exact per-case causes are unavailable in the mounted pair.
parallel_contributors: Parallel used child-agent discovery for CLI and runtime facts, but the parent retained final implementation and verification ownership.
The parent corrected an initial Web Crypto assumption after local `.mjs` execution failed, so that handoff did not remain an unresolved integration error.
The final response acknowledged a program-name output difference in CLI usage/errors while still delivering the solution.
serial_contributors: Serial performed all discovery and implementation locally with no child-agent boundary.
Serial explicitly probed non-ASCII behavior and implemented ASCII JSON escaping before delivery.
Serial also failed the official evaluator at the same 31/70 rate.
ordinary_implementation_differences: The two implementations used different file/module naming conventions and slightly different validation coverage.
Parallel had an initial Web Crypto implementation attempt that required a pure-JS rewrite; serial built a pure-JS path directly.
The mounted final responses and aggregate evaluator records do not expose the hidden cases responsible for the 39 failing samples.
evaluator_effects: Only aggregate official counts are mounted; per-case evaluator cache paths appear only as evidence strings and were not followed.
outcome_analysis.causal_scope: no outcome difference; supported comparative process contrast only

candidates.reason: The parallel parent explicitly implemented the deliverable modules and entry file; child agents were assigned probing work, not ownership of implementation.
There were no independently implemented child components needing integration; the parent assembled one module tree.
The parent created and delivered the required `test10.mjs` entry file and listed it in the final response.
The parent owned the end-to-end path from probing through implementation, repair, testing, and final delivery.
The parent and children probed concurrently, and no single mandatory preflight gate blocked all productive work with an adverse deadline consequence.
Although discovery preceded implementation, the child probes overlapped with parent probing and did not leave implementation unfinished or unverified because of a deferred phase.
No indispensable implementation path was starved; the parent performed the implementation and verification within the run budget.
Parallel used only two visible child task paths and completed without timeout; the official failure was not tied to collective fan-out exhausting the budget.
The child tasks were narrow probes and both returned findings; neither child carried a broad implementation scope that remained unfinished.
The visible child work addressed the delegated CLI and runtime questions; no already-known requirement is shown to be omitted from a child brief and then followed into unusable work.
No child was separately assigned a component that had to interoperate with another child component; children returned observations, and the parent wrote the integrated code.
The child findings that mattered were returned to the parent; there is no before/after evidence that a known finding disappeared during transfer.
The child reports were bounded findings and the parent demonstrably consumed them; no large unstructured report was left materially unprocessed.

The runtime child's Web Crypto finding became a near miss only after the parent tested the actual `.mjs` entry; the parent immediately adjudicated and rewrote the implementation, so no stale handoff caused an unresolved final state.
There were not two incompatible child reports left unresolved. The runtime assumption conflicted with a later local execution failure, and the parent resolved it before closure.

The final response contains a visible acceptance caveat about program-name text, but this is an ordinary acceptance/implementation issue also present in the serial failed outcome, not a parallel-specific completion based on uninspected child or workflow success.
No replacement child or retry repeated work without inherited findings; the parent repaired the Web Crypto failure itself.
